stories.title: America's historic preservation law is in peril, advocates say. Here's what's at stake
stories.summary: It's been exactly 60 years since President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) into law, alongside half a dozen conservation bills. "We have come here this morning to give part of our country back to its people," Johnson declared at the bill signing on Oct. 15, 1966. Now, historic preservation advocates say, the government is trying to yank the public's power away. "Preservation, from its inception, has worked best with public and private partnership," Brent Leggs, the president and CEO of the nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation, told NPR. "Over the last year and a half, the federal government has divested that responsibility."

stories.title: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
stories.summary: With rising temperatures, the buttressing ice shelves at the edges the Antarctic ice sheet are melting and calving off at record rates, leaving behind sheer cliffs of solid ice. The stability of these exposed ice cliffs could influence how Antarctica further breaks apart and contributes to sea level rise around the world. Scientists have assumed that an ice cliff’s stability depends on its height: Ice cliffs that are taller than 100 meters — about the height of the Statue of Liberty — should collapse under their own weight. And once a cliff sloughs off, it should expose even taller, inland cliffs that collapse in turn.
stories.displayTitle: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
stories.originalSummary: The cliffs don’t always collapse in the runaway process that scientists had expected.

stories.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
stories.summary: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information. The research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter endowed associate professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their study, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," was selected as an Editors' Suggestion in Physical Review Letters.

stories.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
stories.summary: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task. Now, researchers at the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME) have built a computational framework that captures the full optical cycle of such spin defects, including the prediction of internal conversion, a process particularly hard to model.

stories.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
stories.summary: Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively. The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats.
stories.displayTitle: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
stories.originalSummary: Scientists have discovered a potential new weapon against a devastating fungus that threatens rice, wheat, and barley worldwide. By engineering a special type of plant immune receptor, researchers created defenses capable of recognizing multiple fungal threats at once. The breakthrough could eventually lead to crops with powerful, long-lasting disease resistance, helping protect a global food supply increasingly threatened by spreading infections and climate change.
stories.explanation: Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats.

reserveStories.summary: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task. reserveStories.title: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
reserveStories.summary: Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively. The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats.

reserveStories.title: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
reserveStories.summary: 2 Min Read Christine E. Giraldo International Space Station Research Communications Team Oct 15, 2026 Article From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s power generation and distribution capability with next-generation International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs). In 2017, a technology demonstration conducted aboard the space station tested the effectiveness of the arrays.

reserveStories.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
reserveStories.summary: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden". A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.

reserveStories.title: Healthy Coral Reversed Bleaching in Its Neighbor With Just 1 Week of Contact
reserveStories.summary: Corals cannot survive long without the algae that live inside their bodies. But under stress from factors like heat, pollution, and UV exposure, these algae can become toxic to the coral, which evicts them. Without their algal symbionts, corals turn white, in what is known as coral bleaching. A 'bleached' coral has limited time to acquire new algal symbionts before it starves to death. With the threat of coral bleaching events growing each year, Stanford scientists have found a technique that could help rescue corals on the brink of death. "While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet," says Stanford marine scientist Danny Collins.
